title: Grief
hookLine: grief is love with nowhere to go, and it takes its own time
tomorrow: can you pray for someone whose family isn't religious?

cards: A second coffee cup set out from habit. A phone number nobody can bring themselves to delete. A voice you still half expect at the door.
Is that okay? Yes. People say grief is love with nowhere to go, and it does strange, ordinary things while it looks for somewhere.
It also keeps its own time, not anyone else's.

teach.h: SIX LINES FROM THE FIELD HOSPITAL TO THE GRAVE.
teach.b: This week walked from the field hospital to the grave. Heal wounds first. Prepare in peace.
Food for the way. Jesus, Mary, Joseph. Stay beside.
The white pall. Grief comes after all of it.

Here's one to tell a friend: one verse in John is only three words long, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And Jesus wept." He's at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, and in the story he's about to raise him. He weeps anyway.
So grief isn't a lack of faith. Paul writes to the Thessalonians about those who have died "that you be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope." He doesn't say don't grieve.
Catholics keep praying for their dead, keep their names, keep a place for them in the Mass. Grief takes its own time because the love didn't end at the funeral.

how: Catholics grieve with prayer for the dead: Masses offered for them, rosaries said in the days after a funeral, names remembered at Mass and in November, the month of the holy souls.

o: love with nowhere to go, in its own time
a phase that ends after the funeral
a weakness that shows a lack of faith

games.q: a week from the field hospital to the grave — tap the pairs.

s: if you believe in heaven, you shouldn't grieve
Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb, and Paul says grieve with hope.
Paul tells the Thessalonians not to be sorrowful as others who have no hope
he doesn't ban grief. he gives it hope.
grief has a timetable, and you're supposed to be done by now
it keeps its own time, because the love didn't end at the funeral.

games.q: a classmate's dad died a while ago. people have stopped asking. on the anniversary, she seems fine. what fits this week's lessons?
o: send a short note: I remember him, and I'm thinking of you.
don't bring it up; it'll only make her sad again.
tell her he's in a better place, so she can let go.
games.why: grief keeps its own time, and the love doesn't end at the funeral. naming the person says it: love continues.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is grieving, recently or long ago; old griefs get forgotten by everyone except the one carrying them. Send a short message with their person's name and that you remember. Then let the sit be for them.

wordCard.voice: Grief. Love with nowhere to go, keeping its own time, and in Catholic hope, still headed somewhere.

carryVoice: Keep this: love continues, the way Jesus wept at the tomb and still called Lazarus out. That's the week.
